checks.question: Are there hard-coded secrets in source code: API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys, connection strings, salts, or other credentials embedded as literals rather than loaded from managed secret storage/config? (CSP-001)

onYes.title: Fix hard-coded secret (CSP-001): move secrets to managed storage and rotate
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Secrets embedded in source are exposed to anyone with repo/artifact access and cannot be rotated easily.

Find all instances: Search source for credential-shaped literals: API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys, connection strings, salts. Look for high-entropy strings and assignments to secret-named variables.

Fix correctly: Move secrets to managed secret storage / configuration (config over hardcoding) and load them at runtime. Treat any exposed value as compromised and rotate it. Add secret scanning to prevent recurrence.

Constraints: Do not commit the new secret anywhere. Never hand-roll crypto or key handling; use the platform's secret/config APIs.

Acceptance: No real secret remains in source; values come from config/secret storage and exposed secrets are rotated. Add a secret-scan gate or test asserting no credential literals are present.

checks.question: Does the codebase write secrets, tokens, passwords, keys, cookies, auth headers, or sensitive config into logs, error messages, or HTTP responses (secret leak in log/error/response)? (CSP-002)

onYes.title: Fix secret leak in log/error/response (CSP-002): redact at source
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Logging or returning secrets exposes them via log stores, error reporters, and client responses.

Find all instances: Search for logging or response serialization of request headers, auth tokens, cookies, passwords, keys, or full config objects. Look for logging whole request/response objects.

Fix correctly: Redact secrets at the source. Use structured logging with a secret-filtering/redaction policy. Serialize responses via explicit DTOs that exclude sensitive fields. Never include secrets in error messages returned to clients.

Constraints: Keep enough non-sensitive context for diagnostics. Do not log full objects that may contain secrets.

Acceptance: No secret is written to logs/errors/responses. Add a test asserting a known secret value does not appear in captured log/response output.

checks.question: Are there real-looking credentials or reusable tokens committed in config, examples, fixtures, docs, snapshots, or tests (secret committed in config/test fixture)? (CSP-003)

onYes.title: Fix committed secret in config/fixtures (CSP-003): replace with fakes and scan
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Credentials in committed config/fixtures/docs are exposed and often still valid.

Find all instances: Search config files, example/sample files, test fixtures, docs, and snapshots for real-looking credentials or reusable tokens.

Fix correctly: Replace with obviously fake, non-functional placeholders. Rotate any exposed real secret. Add a secret-scanning gate to CI.

Constraints: Keep fixtures functional with clearly fake values. Do not just delete the line if code depends on a value; substitute a safe dummy.

Acceptance: No real credential remains in committed files and exposed ones are rotated. Add/enable a secret-scan check.

checks.question: Are security tokens derived from timestamps, counters, hashes of public data, weak PRNGs, or sequential IDs instead of a cryptographically secure RNG (predictable security token)? (CSP-004)

onYes.title: Fix predictable security token (CSP-004): use a CSPRNG with adequate entropy
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Predictable tokens can be guessed/forged, breaking the security control that depends on them.

Find all instances: Search token/secret generation for non-cryptographic RNGs, time/counter-based values, hashes of public data, or sequential IDs.

Fix correctly: Generate tokens with the platform's cryptographically secure RNG and adequate entropy/length. Never hand-roll randomness or crypto.

Constraints: Never roll your own crypto. Config over hardcoding for token length.

Acceptance: All security tokens use a CSPRNG. Add a test asserting generated tokens are unpredictable (non-sequential, expected length/entropy).

checks.question: Does the codebase use obsolete or weak cryptographic primitives: broken ciphers/hashes (e.g. MD5/SHA-1 for security), short key sizes, insecure modes (e.g. ECB), or deprecated signature schemes? (CSP-005)

onYes.title: Fix weak cryptographic primitive (CSP-005): adopt current vetted primitives
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Weak primitives can be broken, forged, or brute-forced, undermining confidentiality/integrity.

Find all instances: Search for use of MD5/SHA-1 (in security contexts), DES/3DES/RC4, ECB mode, short RSA/EC keys, and deprecated signature schemes.

Fix correctly: Replace with current, vetted primitives suitable for the threat model (e.g. SHA-256+ for hashing, AES-GCM or other AEAD for encryption, adequate key sizes). Use the platform's crypto library; never hand-roll.

Constraints: Never roll your own crypto. Provide a migration path for existing data/keys (see CSP-014). Make algorithm choices configurable where feasible.

Acceptance: No weak primitive remains in security-relevant paths. Add a test asserting the expected modern algorithm/key size is used.

checks.question: Does the codebase implement custom/hand-rolled cryptographic protocols, encryption, signing, key exchange, password storage, or token formats instead of using standard reviewed protocols and mature libraries? (CSP-006)

onYes.title: Fix custom crypto protocol (CSP-006): use standard libraries and protocols
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Hand-rolled crypto almost always has subtle, exploitable flaws.

Find all instances: Search for bespoke encryption/signing/key-exchange/password-hashing/token-format code (manual XOR, custom MACs, custom KDFs, custom handshake logic).

Fix correctly: Replace with standard, reviewed protocols and mature vetted libraries (e.g. the platform crypto APIs, established OAuth/OIDC/JWT libraries, a standard password KDF). Remove the custom implementation.

Constraints: Never roll your own crypto. Check library licenses before adopting (avoid problematic copyleft/commercial-tier where the project bars them). Migrate existing data safely.

Acceptance: Custom crypto is replaced by a vetted library/protocol. Add tests proving interop/round-trip correctness with the standard implementation.

checks.question: Is sensitive data transmitted over unencrypted HTTP, raw sockets, insecure protocols, or with TLS disabled, rather than requiring encrypted transport that fails closed (missing transport encryption)? (CSP-007)

onYes.title: Fix missing transport encryption (CSP-007): require TLS and fail closed
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Sending sensitive data in cleartext exposes it to network eavesdropping and tampering.

Find all instances: Search for http:// endpoints handling sensitive data, raw/plaintext sockets, and protocols/clients with encryption disabled or optional.

Fix correctly: Require encrypted transport (TLS) for sensitive data; redirect/upgrade to HTTPS; fail closed when secure transport is unavailable rather than silently downgrading.

Constraints: Do not provide an insecure fallback. Config over hardcoding for endpoints.

Acceptance: Sensitive data flows only over encrypted transport. Add a test/config check asserting plaintext transport is rejected for sensitive paths.

checks.question: Does the codebase disable TLS certificate validation, hostname verification, or use trust-all callbacks / insecure TLS flags (TLS verification disabled)? (CSP-008)

onYes.title: Fix disabled TLS verification (CSP-008): enable cert and hostname validation
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Disabling certificate/hostname validation allows trivial man-in-the-middle attacks.

Find all instances: Search for trust-all certificate callbacks, disabled hostname verification, insecure/skip-verify flags, and custom trust managers that accept everything.

Fix correctly: Enable full certificate chain and hostname validation using the default trust store. If a custom CA is needed, add that specific CA to the trust configuration rather than disabling validation.

Constraints: Never roll your own TLS validation. No 'accept all' shortcuts, even for tests against real endpoints.

Acceptance: All TLS clients validate chain and hostname. Add a test/check asserting connections to an untrusted/mismatched certificate are rejected.

checks.question: Does certificate validation only partially verify trust: ignoring expiry, pinning incorrectly, trusting arbitrary roots, or skipping key-usage/revocation where required (incomplete certificate trust validation)? (CSP-009)

onYes.title: Fix incomplete certificate validation (CSP-009): validate the full trust chain
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Partial certificate validation leaves MITM gaps even when validation appears present.

Find all instances: Search certificate validation code for missing chain/hostname/expiry checks, incorrect or hard-coded pins, arbitrary root trust, and missing key-usage/revocation checks where required.

Fix correctly: Validate chain, hostname, expiry/not-before, key usage, and (where required) revocation. Implement pinning correctly with a rotation strategy if used.

Constraints: Never roll your own crypto/validation; rely on platform validation and only add specific, intentional trust.

Acceptance: Certificate validation is complete and correct. Add tests for expired, wrong-host, and untrusted-root certificates proving rejection.

checks.question: Does the codebase encrypt with constant IVs, repeated/deterministic nonces, or otherwise reuse a nonce/IV with the same key (static IV / nonce reuse)? (CSP-010)

onYes.title: Fix static IV / nonce reuse (CSP-010): generate unique nonces per encryption
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Reusing IVs/nonces with the same key breaks confidentiality (and integrity for AEAD), often catastrophically.

Find all instances: Search encryption calls for hard-coded/constant IVs, fixed/deterministic nonces, or nonces derived from predictable counters reused across messages with the same key.

Fix correctly: Generate a unique IV/nonce per encryption as required by the algorithm (random for CBC; unique-per-key for GCM/AEAD), using a secure RNG, and transmit/store it alongside the ciphertext.

Constraints: Never roll your own crypto. Follow the specific algorithm's nonce requirements.

Acceptance: Every encryption uses a unique, correctly generated IV/nonce. Add a test asserting two encryptions of the same plaintext produce different ciphertext/IVs.

checks.question: Does the codebase encrypt data without authenticating it (no AEAD and no separate MAC over ciphertext and metadata), leaving encryption without integrity? (CSP-011)

onYes.title: Fix encryption without integrity (CSP-011): use authenticated encryption
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Unauthenticated encryption is vulnerable to tampering and padding-oracle style attacks.

Find all instances: Search for encryption that lacks integrity: raw CBC/CTR without a MAC, or any cipher use without authentication over ciphertext and associated metadata.

Fix correctly: Use authenticated encryption (AEAD such as AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305), or add a MAC (encrypt-then-MAC) over the ciphertext and relevant metadata, verified before decryption.

Constraints: Never roll your own crypto. Verify integrity before using decrypted data.

Acceptance: Encrypted data is authenticated. Add a test that flips a ciphertext byte and asserts decryption fails integrity verification.

checks.question: Are passwords stored using fast/general-purpose hashes (e.g. plain SHA-256/MD5), reversible encryption, or encoding, instead of a dedicated password KDF (plain hash for password storage)? (CSP-012)

onYes.title: Fix password storage hashing (CSP-012): use a password KDF with work factor
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Fast or reversible password storage lets attackers crack or recover passwords quickly after a breach.

Find all instances: Search password persistence for fast hashes (MD5/SHA-x), encoding (base64), or reversible encryption used to store passwords.

Fix correctly: Use a dedicated password KDF (e.g. Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt) with a unique per-password salt and an appropriate, configurable work factor. Migrate existing hashes safely (rehash on next successful login).

Constraints: Never roll your own crypto; use a vetted KDF library. Config over hardcoding for the work factor.

Acceptance: Passwords are stored with a proper KDF + salt. Add tests asserting a verifiable hash format and that verification works; include the migration path.

checks.question: Are password hashes stored without a unique per-password salt (unsalted password hash)? (CSP-013)

onYes.title: Fix unsalted password hash (CSP-013): add unique per-password salts
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Unsalted hashes are vulnerable to rainbow-table and bulk-cracking attacks and reveal duplicate passwords.

Find all instances: Search password hashing for missing or shared/static salts.

Fix correctly: Use a password KDF that generates and stores a unique per-password salt (most KDFs do this in their output format). Migrate existing unsalted hashes safely (rehash on next login).

Constraints: Never roll your own crypto. Store the salt with the hash via the KDF's standard format.

Acceptance: Every password hash has a unique salt. Add a test asserting two users with the same password produce different stored hashes.

checks.question: Do encryption/signing keys lack versioning, rotation, revocation, or a migration strategy (missing key rotation path)? (CSP-014)

onYes.title: Fix missing key rotation path (CSP-014): add key IDs, versioning, and rotation
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Without rotation/versioning, a compromised key cannot be retired without breaking existing data.

Find all instances: Search key management for hard-coded single keys, no key IDs/versioning, and no rotation/revocation/migration support.

Fix correctly: Introduce key IDs and versioning; tag ciphertext/signatures with the key version. Support dual-read (decrypt with old, encrypt with new) and a re-encryption/migration path. Store keys in managed key storage.

Constraints: Never roll your own crypto/key handling; use a KMS/key-store where available. Config over hardcoding for active key selection.

Acceptance: Keys are versioned and rotatable with a migration path. Add a test proving data encrypted under an old key version still decrypts after rotation.

checks.question: Does the codebase collect, store, or transmit personal data not required by the product or a legal purpose (excessive personal data collection)? (CSP-015)

onYes.title: Fix excessive personal data collection (CSP-015): minimize collected data
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Collecting unnecessary personal data increases breach impact and compliance burden.

Find all instances: Search data models, request handlers, and integrations for personal data fields collected/stored/transmitted without a clear product or legal need.

Fix correctly: Remove or stop persisting unneeded personal fields. For each sensitive field that remains, document its purpose. Apply data minimization end to end (intake, storage, logs, analytics).

Constraints: Do not break features that genuinely need a field; justify those. Coordinate with retention/deletion (CSP-018).

Acceptance: Only justified personal data is collected/stored. Add/adjust tests for the trimmed data model and confirm no removed field is still persisted.

checks.question: Is sensitive data stored in databases, files, caches, queues, backups, or logs without encryption at rest (sensitive data unencrypted at rest)? (CSP-016)

onYes.title: Fix sensitive data unencrypted at rest (CSP-016): encrypt high-risk data
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Sensitive data stored in cleartext is fully exposed if storage/backups are compromised.

Find all instances: Search for high-risk data (credentials, tokens, financial, health, PII) persisted to DB/files/caches/queues/backups/logs without encryption.

Fix correctly: Encrypt high-risk data at rest (field-level or storage-level as appropriate), with keys managed separately from the data (see CSP-014). Avoid storing sensitive data in logs at all.

Constraints: Never roll your own crypto. Manage keys in a key store. Coordinate with rotation.

Acceptance: High-risk data is encrypted at rest with separately managed keys. Add a test/check confirming the stored representation is not cleartext.

checks.question: Does the codebase send personal data, identifiers, addresses, health/payment data, or user content to analytics/telemetry/logs without redaction (PII emitted to analytics/logs)? (CSP-017)

onYes.title: Fix PII emitted to telemetry (CSP-017): redact or omit PII
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Sending PII to analytics/telemetry/logs leaks it to third parties and widens exposure.

Find all instances: Search analytics/telemetry/logging calls for personal identifiers, addresses, health/payment data, or raw user content.

Fix correctly: Redact, tokenize, aggregate, or safely hash PII before emission, or avoid collecting it. Centralize a telemetry redaction policy.

Constraints: Keep telemetry useful via non-identifying aggregates. Avoid high-cardinality identifiers as labels (see OPS-017).

Acceptance: No raw PII reaches analytics/telemetry/logs. Add a test asserting a PII value is redacted/omitted from emitted telemetry.

checks.question: Is personal or sensitive data stored without deletion, expiry, retention, or legal-hold handling (missing retention/deletion enforcement)? (CSP-018)

onYes.title: Fix missing retention/deletion (CSP-018): enforce lifecycle deletion policy
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Indefinitely retained personal data increases breach and compliance risk and may violate the law.

Find all instances: Search stores of personal/sensitive data for the presence of retention/expiry/deletion logic and legal-hold handling.

Fix correctly: Implement lifecycle deletion and retention policy enforcement (TTL/scheduled purges, user-initiated deletion that cascades to derived data, backups, and logs), with legal-hold exceptions.

Constraints: Config over hardcoding for retention windows. Ensure deletion reaches caches/backups/derived stores.

Acceptance: Personal data has enforced retention/deletion. Add a test proving data is purged after its retention window / on deletion request.

checks.question: Are exports, backups, reports, or downloads exposed through public links, weak auth, or long-lived URLs (insecure export/backup exposure)? (CSP-019)

onYes.title: Fix insecure export/backup exposure (CSP-019): restrict, expire, and audit
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Publicly reachable or long-lived export/backup URLs leak bulk sensitive data.

Find all instances: Search export/backup/report/download features for public links, weak/no auth, and long-lived or guessable URLs.

Fix correctly: Require authentication and authorization for exports/downloads; use short-lived, signed, single-use URLs; encrypt exports/backups; and audit download access.

Constraints: Authorize per-object (see IAM-006). Config over hardcoding for link lifetimes.

Acceptance: Exports/backups require auth and use short-lived access with audit logging. Add a test proving an unauthorized or expired export link is rejected.

checks.question: Does the codebase perform sensitive processing, analytics, notifications, data sharing, or profiling without checking consent, jurisdiction, or purpose (missing consent/purpose check)? (CSP-020)

onYes.title: Fix missing consent/purpose check (CSP-020): gate processing on consent
onYes.prompt:
Problem: Processing personal data without consent/purpose gating can violate privacy law and user trust.

Find all instances: Search analytics, notifications, data-sharing, and profiling code paths for consent/jurisdiction/purpose checks before processing.

Fix correctly: Enforce consent, jurisdiction, and purpose checks before sensitive processing. Centralize the consent decision and honor withdrawal.

Constraints: Default to not processing when consent is unknown. Config over hardcoding for jurisdiction rules.

Acceptance: Sensitive processing is gated on consent/purpose. Add a test proving processing is skipped when consent is absent/withdrawn.
